newsitem.title: UK: ROWING-HENLEY: SOCIAL WHIRL OR SPORTING OCCASION?.
newsitem.headline: ROWING-HENLEY: SOCIAL WHIRL OR SPORTING OCCASION?.

text.p: If you can see beyond the brightly-coloured blazers, old school ties and extravagant hats you might notice there is a river in Henley and occasionally boats racing up and down on it.

Henley Royal Regatta, an annual five-day event in a small town some 30 miles west of London, is perhaps better known for its place in the British social season than as a date on the rowing calendar but crews from all over the world come to compete for the prestige of a Henley medal.
The regatta is held on the Thames over the first weekend in July, coming after Ascot and coinciding with Wimbledon -- two other events which mix social and sporting status.

Henley is probably the only place in the world where your car parking space -- often handed down through families -- is as much a status symbol as the clothes you wear. Places in the field closest to the regatta enclosures are coveted for their proximity to the course and their high visibility.

Caterers Letheby and Christopher, who have been at the Henley event for the last three years, estimated that up until Saturday -- the most popular day for socialising and spectating -- they had sold around 1,000 kgs of strawberries, 5,000 bottles of champagne and 15,000 pints of Pimms.

The atmosphere of an Edwardian garden party is perpetuated by "style police", security guards who stand at the entrance of the elite Stewards' Enclosure checking that women are wearing skirts that fall below the knee and men are wearing jackets and ties.

Colourful blazers ranging from the bright purple of University of London to the deep cerise of Leander, Britain's most prestigious rowing club, are worn proudly to show allegiance and also credibility.

Entry to the Stewards' Enclosure, which is located at the finish of the race course, can be gained only by those wearing special badges which are limited in number and can be obtained only through a member of the Stewards -- the all-male committee who run Henley.
Henley is first and foremost a sporting event but this very British affair does see all racing stop for an hour-and-a-half at lunch and an hour in mid-afternoon for tea.
Further down the course the atmosphere is more like a camping site, with vans selling hamburgers and pizzas and most people wearing T-shirts and shorts.

But beyond the social one-upmanship is a fiercely competitive regatta involving crews ranging from schoolboys to Olympic gold medallists. Henley is perhaps unique in entertaining such a diversity of crews and abilities and for many clubs and schools it is the highlight of their rowing year.
Those who compete and organise the regatta say they do not resent the social side and do not see it as detracting from the rowing.

Steve Redgrave, Britain's four-times Olympic gold medallist said: "I don't see the social side as a problem -- the rowing came first and without that there would be no social occasion so the one created the other."
Redgrave says that for many Henley is their first experience of rowing and serves to broaden its appeal.
David Tanner, international manager of the Amateur Rowing Association (ARA) said: "It's run as a very good business and has managed to modernise while still keeping its traditions."
"People come here to do what they want to do but it's great because it encourages people to come and have a look -- especially young people."
The regatta is also profitable for the town, with restaurants, pubs and hotels filled to bursting point for five days.

Henley Royal Regatta is not run principally as a commercial enterprise but officials estimate it costs around 1.3 million pounds ($2.2 million) to stage and generates income of 1.5 million pounds ($2.5 million).
Much of the profit is ploughed back into the sport, supporting many rowing projects over the last five years and particularly encouraging the development of junior rowing.
But for many, such as one young woman who on entering the Stewards' Enclosure turned to her companion and said: "I didn't know there was a river here!", rowing is not always the highest priority.
